title: Supply-Chain Attacks on AI

title: Supporting Articles
description: Articles that back up a pillar or keystone
body_head: # Supporting Articles  ## Summary Supporting articles are the pages beneath a pillar or keystone — each covers one facet the pillar references rather than duplicating.  ## Details - Their relationship to the pillar is explicit: the pillar links them, they link back, and the cluster reads as one unit. - Supporting articles are where most of the wiki's depth actually lives; pillars are the summary layer. - For mykb, supporting articles are the default promotion targets once a pillar exists.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/pillar-pages|Pillar Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/supporting-articles|Supporting Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-articles|Keystone Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/parent-child

title: Surface Similarity
description: Similarity based on superficial features rather than structure
body_head: # Surface Similarity  ## Summary  Surface Similarity — Similarity based on superficial features rather than structure. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Surface similarity is fast, salient, and often misleading. - Novices rely on it; experts learn to look past it. - Classic problem-solving studies: story solutions transfer only when surface stories match. - Contrast with relational similarity and deep structure.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/relational-similarity|Relational Similarity]] — deep counterpart - [[wiki/concepts/analogical-transfer|Analogical Transfer]] — failure cause - [[wiki/concepts/similarity-base

title: Survivorship Bias
description: Drawing conclusions only from those who made it through selection
body_head: # Survivorship Bias  ## Summary  Survivorship bias is the error of drawing conclusions from a set of survivors — cases that passed a selection process — while ignoring the cases that did not. It matters because the invisible non-survivors often carry the most information, and ignoring them flatters the survivors' apparent qualities. Classic examples range from WWII planes to startup advice.  ## Details  - **Definition** — When analysis conditions on survival, the sample is systematically selected, and inferred causes of survival are confounded by the selection process. - **Classic example** — Armoring the parts of returning aircraft where they were most damaged ignored the planes that did

title: Sustained Attention
description: Maintaining focus on a task over extended periods
body_head: # Sustained Attention  ## Summary  Sustained Attention — Maintaining focus on a task over extended periods. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Sustained attention supports long tasks: monitoring, listening, studying. - Performance declines over time unless the task is engaging. - Mind-wandering marks lapses in sustained attention. - Links to vigilance-decrement and to flow state.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/vigilance-decrement|Vigilance Decrement]] — the decline curve - [[wiki/concepts/selective-attention|Selective Attention]] — focus mechanism - [[wiki/meta-learning/flow-state|Flow State]] — optimal engagement

title: Systematic Review
description: Explicit, reproducible method for collecting and appraising all relevant studies
body_head: # Systematic Review  ## Summary  A systematic review is a methodical synthesis of research that uses explicit, reproducible procedures to find, appraise, and combine all relevant studies on a question. It matters because it replaces cherry-picked summaries with a transparent evidence base, and it exposes gaps and biases in the literature. Systematic reviews are the foundation of evidence-based practice.  ## Details  - **Definition** — A systematic review specifies eligibility criteria, search strategies, and appraisal methods in advance, then applies them uniformly. - **Protocol** — A pre-registered protocol defines the question, databases, inclusion rules, and analysis plan, limiting post

title: Tag Cascade
description: The ripple of changes a tag operation triggers across articles
body_head: # Tag Cascade  ## Summary A tag cascade is the full set of article edits produced by one tag operation — merge, split, or rename — propagated to every affected file.  ## Details - Cascades are why tag operations are batched and dry-run first: a small decision can touch dozens of articles. - The cascade is complete only when the global tag report shows no stragglers using old or orphaned tags. - For mykb, the tag cascade is the mechanical layer underneath tag hygiene, and its verification is part of the audit checklist.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tag-merging|Tag Merging]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-splitting|Tag Splitting]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-renaming|Tag Renaming]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-h

title: Tag Hygiene
description: Keeping the tag vocabulary clean, consistent, and useful
body_head: # Tag Hygiene  ## Summary Tag hygiene is the ongoing work of keeping the tag set small, consistent, and meaningful: no singular/plural pairs, no typos, no near-duplicate tags.  ## Details - A dirty tag vocabulary silently fragments clusters — two tags that look alike never group their articles together. - Hygiene is enforced by reports (tag counts, near-duplicate detection) and repaired by tag merging and tag renaming. - For mykb, tag hygiene runs as a periodic audit between curation sprints.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tags-practice|Tags Practice]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-merging|Tag Merging]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-renaming|Tag Renaming]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-splitting|Tag Splitting]] -

title: Tag Merging
description: Combining two tags that mean the same thing into one
body_head: # Tag Merging  ## Summary Tag merging collapses near-duplicate tags (like singular and plural forms, or hyphenated and unhyphenated variants) into a single canonical tag.  ## Details - A merge rewrites the tag across every article that uses either variant, so the cluster reforms correctly. - Merge decisions are recorded so future curators do not reintroduce the split spelling. - For mykb, tag merging is part of tag hygiene and is usually batched after a tag report reveals the duplicates.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tag-hygiene|Tag Hygiene]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-splitting|Tag Splitting]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-renaming|Tag Renaming]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-cascade|Tag Cascade]] - [[wiki/co

title: Tag Renaming
description: Changing a tag's name while keeping its articles together
body_head: # Tag Renaming  ## Summary Tag renaming changes a tag's label to a better canonical name, rewriting every article that uses it in one pass.  ## Details - Renames are preferable to creating a new tag and leaving the old one behind — the old tag would linger with a fraction of the articles. - The rename should be recorded (old name, new name, date) so search and future reports map history correctly. - For mykb, tag renames follow the same review discipline as slug changes: batch, dry-run, verify.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tag-merging|Tag Merging]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-hygiene|Tag Hygiene]] - [[wiki/concepts/tags-practice|Tags Practice]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-cascade|Tag Cascade]] - [[wi

title: Tag Splitting
description: Dividing one overloaded tag into two precise ones
body_head: # Tag Splitting  ## Summary Tag splitting divides a tag that has accumulated two distinct meanings — for example a tag covering both tooling and practice — into two precise tags.  ## Details - The trigger is scale and ambiguity: when reading a tag's articles no longer yields a coherent set, the tag has lost its meaning. - A split requires deciding each article's side, so it is a reviewed, batched operation with a tag-cascade check afterward. - For mykb, tag splits are rarer than merges and usually follow a tag-suggestions report showing two clusters inside one tag.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tag-merging|Tag Merging]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-cascade|Tag Cascade]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-sugg

title: Tag Suggestions
description: Automated proposals for tags an article is missing
body_head: # Tag Suggestions  ## Summary Tag suggestions derive candidate tags for an article from its text and from tags used by similar articles, closing the gap where authors forgot or never knew the vocabulary.  ## Details - Suggestions are advisory: the pipeline proposes, a human accepts, because an automated tag can be confidently wrong. - The suggestions model is only as good as the tag hygiene underneath it — a dirty vocabulary trains bad suggestions. - For mykb, tag suggestions feed the curation review queue and keep new articles in the existing cluster structure.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tags-practice|Tags Practice]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-hygiene|Tag Hygiene]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-mer

title: Tags Practice
description: The conventions for choosing and applying tags to articles
body_head: # Tags Practice  ## Summary Tags practice defines how tags are chosen: a controlled vocabulary, 3-5 tags per article, each tag naming a real cluster rather than restating the title.  ## Details - Good tags are stable, plural-ish nouns that group genuinely related articles; bad tags are one-off words that never repeat. - Tags are metadata, not a substitute for links — a tag should point at a category, while a link points at a specific article. - For mykb, tags practice is enforced by tag-hygiene checks and the tag suggestions pipeline.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/tag-hygiene|Tag Hygiene]] - [[wiki/concepts/tag-suggestions|Tag Suggestions]] - [[wiki/concepts/tags-practice|Tags Practice]] -

title: Tail Risks
description: Low-probability, high-impact outcomes
body_head: # Tail Risks  ## Summary Tail risks are outcomes in the far tails of probability distributions: rare and severe. The concept matters because standard decision-making — averages, most-likely scenarios, Gaussian intuition — systematically ignores the tails, and for AI the tails are where the catastrophic outcomes live: a small probability of enormous harm can dominate every other consideration in the expected-value calculation.  ## Details - The mathematical shape: in a Gaussian distribution, tail events are exponentially rare — 6-sigma events essentially never happen, so ignoring them is rational. title: Takeoff Scenarios
description: Contrasting stories about the speed and controllability of AI capability growth
body_head: # Takeoff Scenarios  ## Summary Takeoff scenarios are stylized futures for how quickly AI systems go from roughly human-level to far beyond: slow/continuous, fast/explosive, or moderate. They matter because they determine whether oversight, verification, and governance can keep pace with capability.  ## Details - **Slow takeoff** — capabilities rise smoothly with economic and regulatory adaptation; many fixes stay viable. - **Fast takeoff** — recursive self-improvement compounds in weeks or days, outrunning any review process. - **Moderate takeoff** — episodic jumps (new training paradigm, self-improving scaffold) separated by plateaus. - **Policy import** — most governance levers (evals,

title: Talk Pages
description: The classic discussion page attached to an article
body_head: # Talk Pages  ## Summary Talk pages are the discussion space attached to each article, where editors hash out disagreements before editing the page itself.  ## Details - The convention is to talk first for contested changes: propose, discuss, then edit with the discussion's conclusion. - Talk pages need hygiene — sign, thread, close — or they become unreadable archives of indecision. - For mykb, talk pages are used sparingly and their conclusions are recorded in edit summaries.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/discussion-pages|Discussion Pages]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/edit-summaries-wiki|Edit Summaries]] - [[wiki/concepts/consensus-wiki|Consensus]] - [[wiki/concepts/talk-pages|Talk Pages]] - [[wi

title: Task Lists
description: Structured lists of work items for the wiki
body_head: # Task Lists  ## Summary Task lists are the wiki's work inventory: each item names the task, the target article, the requester, and the acceptance criteria.  ## Details - They convert flagged problems (cleanup-needed, sources-needed) into assignable work with state. - A task list without triage is just a pile — priority and effort labels turn it into a queue. - For mykb, task lists are the execution layer under the review queues and curation sprints.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/todo-lists|Todo Lists]] - [[wiki/concepts/task-lists-wiki|Task Lists]] - [[wiki/agent-systems/triage-workflow|Triage Workflow]] - [[wiki/agent-systems/queue-management|Queue Management]] - [[wiki/concepts/wiki-tas

title: Task Robustness
description: Performance stability across task variations
body_head: # Task Robustness  ## Summary Task robustness is consistent competence across variations of a task: different data, formats, and edge cases.  ## Details - Task robustness is consistent competence across variations of a task: different data, formats, and edge cases. - It is measured by benchmark suites that sample task space. - High task robustness on benchmarks still fails to guarantee novel tasks. - RSIS3 relevance: the bundle's tools would be re-run across varied wiki states each pass.  - Measurement: benchmark suites sample the task space — variations in data, format, and edge cases — and robustness is the spread of performance across those samples, not the score on any single one. - Ro

title: Workspace Telemetry
description: Structured, append-only event records of every loop action — the audit trail that makes self-improvement observable
body_head: # Workspace Telemetry  ## Summary Workspace telemetry is the append-only record of everything a self-improving system does: loop starts, tool calls, evaluations, completions, and errors, each with a timestamp and structured metadata. It matters because a system that rewrites itself is only trustworthy if every mutation is observable and replayable from logs. In RSIS3 every loop writes telemetry events (l1_start … l9_complete) to `.rsis/telemetry/*.jsonl`, one file per session.  ## Details - **Event shape**: `type`, `timestamp`, and loop-specific metadata (cycle, decision, deltas, stats). title: Temperature Scaling
description: Adjusting output sharpness for better confidence
body_head: # Temperature Scaling  ## Summary Temperature scaling divides logits by a temperature to soften or sharpen probability outputs.  ## Details - Temperature scaling divides logits by a temperature to soften or sharpen probability outputs. - It is the standard post-hoc calibration fix for classifiers. - LLM sampling temperature trades creativity for determinism. - RSIS3 relevance: retrieval confidence thresholds are temperature-like knobs on the graph.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/calibration|Calibration]] — the property - [[wiki/concepts/label-smoothing|Label Smoothing]] — the training-side twin - [[wiki/agent-systems/self-evaluation|Self-Evaluation]] — the confidence link - [[wiki/decisions

title: Temporal Difference Learning
description: Learning from the difference between successive value estimates
body_head: # Temporal Difference Learning  ## Summary Temporal difference (TD) learning updates value estimates from the difference between successive predictions, without waiting for the final outcome. It matters because it learns online, step by step. It is the backbone of modern reinforcement learning.  ## Details - The insight that made TD learning revolutionary: you do not need the final outcome to learn. After taking a step from state s to s', the agent receives reward r and can immediately compare its prediction for s (V(s)) with its updated prediction for s' (r + γV(s')). title: Terminal Goals
description: Goals pursued for their own sake
body_head: # Terminal Goals  ## Summary Terminal goals are objectives valued intrinsically, not as means to something else.  ## Details - Terminal goals are objectives valued intrinsically, not as means to something else. - A system's terminal goals define what it ultimately optimizes; everything else is instrumental. - Specifying terminal goals well is the crux of alignment (value specification). - RSIS3 relevance: the identity system states the workspace's terminal purpose.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/instrumental-goals|Instrumental Goals]] — the means - [[wiki/concepts/goal-content-thesis|Goal Content Thesis]] — what goals look like - [[wiki/concepts/value-specification|Value Specification]] — t

title: Test Set Leakage
description: Test data accidentally influencing training or decisions
body_head: # Test Set Leakage  ## Summary Test set leakage is any channel through which test data influences training, tuning, or reporting.  ## Details - Test set leakage is any channel through which test data influences training, tuning, or reporting. - Channels include web scrapes, human review, and shared embeddings. - Leakage is usually invisible in scores — it just makes them lie. - RSIS3 relevance: leaked pass expectations would let the generator 'cheat' the verifier.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/train-test-contamination|Train-Test Contamination]] — the direct form - [[wiki/decisions/eval-splits|Eval Splits]] — the barrier - [[wiki/concepts/benchmark-contamination|Benchmark Contamination]] —

title: Time-Sensitive Content
description: Content whose correctness expires with time
body_head: # Time-Sensitive Content  ## Summary Time-sensitive content is material that is correct now and wrong later: version numbers, prices, security statuses, API names.  ## Details - The discipline is labeling: 'as of', 'current version', and dated-claims markers make the expiration visible to readers. - Curation treats time-sensitive content as a liability class with its own review cadence, shorter than evergreen. - For mykb, time-sensitive content is flagged at review time and drives the timeliness-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/dated-claims|Dated Claims]] - [[wiki/concepts/timeliness-score|Timeliness Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/timely-articles|Timely Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/time-sen

title: Timeliness Score
description: The sub-score rating how current an article is
body_head: # Timeliness Score  ## Summary The timeliness score rates how current an article is: source dates, dated claims, review status, and the freshness of fast-moving content.  ## Details - It is computed from the freshness signals — the difference between now and the article's review date, weighted by how fast the topic decays. - A low timeliness score triggers refresh-days work, not demotion — staleness is fixable. - For mykb, the timeliness score is the dashboard's canary for content rot.  ## Related - [[wiki/ai-ml/score-components|Score Components]] - [[wiki/concepts/timeliness-score|Timeliness Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/freshness-signals|Freshness Signals]] - [[wiki/concepts/stale-articles|S

title: Timely Articles
description: Articles whose value depends on being current
body_head: # Timely Articles  ## Summary Timely articles are valuable only while current — tool releases, security advisories, ecosystem shifts — and decay fast after.  ## Details - They need the tightest freshness cadence and should be written shortform to make that cheap. - A timely article that goes stale is worse than none: it confidently describes a world that no longer exists. - For mykb, timely articles carry the timeliness-score and are first candidates for update-days.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/evergreen-articles|Evergreen Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/timely-articles|Timely Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/timeliness-score|Timeliness Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/content-freshness-review|Content

title: Todo Lists

body_head: # Todo Lists  ## Summary Todo lists are the lightweight side of task management: checklists of pending work that live with the person or sprint doing them.  ## Details - They work when they are short, current, and tied to an owner; a stale todo list is a liability. - Todo lists differ from task lists in formality — todos are for the worker, tasks are for the system. - For mykb, todo lists feed edit sprints and are consolidated into task lists when work crosses sessions.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/task-lists-wiki|Task Lists]] - [[wiki/concepts/todo-lists|Todo Lists]] - [[wiki/devops-infra/edit-sprints|Edit Sprints]] - [[wiki/concepts/wiki-tasks|Wiki Tasks]] - [[wiki/agent-systems/queue-m

title: Tolerance of Ambiguity
description: Comfort with uncertain, incomplete, or contradictory situations
body_head: # Tolerance of Ambiguity  ## Summary  Tolerance of ambiguity is the disposition to accept and operate within situations that are uncertain, incomplete, or contradictory without excessive discomfort. It matters because much real work — research, leadership, product development — is inherently ambiguous, and low tolerance drives premature closure or avoidance. It varies across people, contexts, and training, and interacts with risk preferences.  ## Details  - **Definition** — The construct captures how people respond when information is missing, conflicting, or complex enough to resist neat resolution. - **Consequences** — Low tolerance correlates with dogmatic conclusions, black-and-white t

title: Top-Down Processing

body_head: # Top-Down Processing  ## Summary  Top-Down Processing — Perception and cognition shaped by expectations, knowledge, and context. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Top-down signals fill in ambiguous input using priors and schemas. - Explains why context disambiguates words, scenes, and faces. - Can generate errors: expectations override weak bottom-up evidence. - Complement of bottom-up processing; perception uses both.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/bottom-up-processing|Bottom-Up Processing]] — data-driven complement - [[wiki/concepts/predictive-processing|Predictive Processing]] — modern framework - [[wiki/memor

title: Topic Pages
description: Pages that organize articles around a subject area
body_head: # Topic Pages  ## Summary Topic pages organize a subject area: a lead summary, the key articles, and links to subtopics, giving newcomers a place to start.  ## Details - Unlike category pages, topic pages are curated — they choose and order, rather than dump every tag match. - A topic page is a small synthesis: it asserts how the area is structured, so it needs maintenance as the area grows. - For mykb, topic pages are the top of the parent-child hierarchy and are written deliberately, not generated.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/category-pages|Category Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/topic-pages|Topic Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/overview-pages|Overview Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/hub-pages|Hub Page

title: Train-Test Contamination

body_head: # Train-Test Contamination  ## Summary Train-test contamination occurs when evaluation examples appear (directly or near-duplicate) in training data.  ## Details - Train-test contamination occurs when evaluation examples appear (directly or near-duplicate) in training data. - It inflates benchmark scores and masks true generalization. - Detection uses duplicate and near-duplicate search against training corpora. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's eval of retrieval quality must exclude pages used to build the index.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/benchmark-contamination|Benchmark Contamination]] — the benchmark form - [[wiki/concepts/eval-contamination|Eval Contamination]] — the broad form - [[wi

title: Transformative AI

title: TransformerLens

title: Trojan Attacks
description: Models carrying hidden malicious behavior from training
body_head: # Trojan Attacks  ## Summary Trojan attacks embed hidden malicious behavior into models during training or fine-tuning, activated by specific inputs. The defining feature is a trigger: the model behaves normally on ordinary inputs and switches to malicious behavior only when the trigger appears — a pattern in the image, a token sequence in the prompt, or a rare input condition — making the compromise nearly invisible until activated.  ## Details - The mechanism: during training or fine-tuning, the attacker controls the data (or the training process) and injects examples pairing the trigger with the malicious behavior. title: Tuning Oscillation
description: The thrash signal: a tuned loop flips its adjustments back and forth, and the meta-tuner widens the deadband
body_head: # Tuning Oscillation  ## Summary Tuning oscillation is the pattern where a loop's adjustments alternate sign across cycles — up, down, up, down — because its response threshold is too tight around the equilibrium. It is a stability signal: the loop is reacting to noise instead of trend. The meta-tuner responds by widening the deadband so the loop stops thrashing. RSIS3 uses this in two places: L7 widens L4's success deadband on oscillating deltas, and L9 widens L6's identity band on alternating shrink/grow.  ## Details - **Detection**: look at accepted history entries; if consecutive deltas alternate sign (+, −, +), classify as oscillation. - **Response**: widen the band — L7 moves `target

title: Tuning Ownership Diagonal
description: The +3 rule: loop k+3 tunes loop k, so every parameter has exactly one writer
body_head: # Tuning Ownership Diagonal  ## Summary The tuning ownership diagonal is the rule that resolves overlapping loops: loop k+3 tunes loop k. L4→L1, L5→L2, L6→L3, L7→L4, L8→L5, L9→L6. title: Umbrella Articles
description: Articles that cover a family of related concepts
body_head: # Umbrella Articles  ## Summary Umbrella articles cover a family of related concepts, providing the shared framing and the links to each member.  ## Details - They are the parent in the parent-child hierarchy: the umbrella gives the map, the children give the detail. - Umbrellas fail when they absorb their children's content instead of linking it — the umbrella should summarize, not duplicate. - For mykb, umbrella articles are a natural fit for topic pages and category pages.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/umbrella-articles|Umbrella Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/parent-child-articles|Parent-Child Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/topic-pages|Topic Pages]] - [[wiki/concepts/category-pages|Category

title: Uncertainty Management
description: Practices for identifying, quantifying, and acting under uncertainty
body_head: # Uncertainty Management  ## Summary Uncertainty management is the discipline of naming what is unknown, estimating its size, and deciding anyway. It spans aleatory and epistemic uncertainty, probability calibration, and hedging. Knowledge systems that store uncertainty improve decisions without pretending to certainty.  ## Details - **Two types** — aleatory (irreducible chance) and epistemic (missing knowledge). - **Tools** — intervals, probabilities, scenarios, and decision rules. - **Culture** — admitting uncertainty is a precondition for managing it. - **In mykb** — confidence fields and open questions operationalize it.  ## Related - [[wiki/questions/aleatory-vs-epistemic|Aleatory vs

title: Under Review
description: The state marking an article currently being reviewed
body_head: # Under Review  ## Summary Under-review marks an article that a reviewer has checked out and is actively working on, preventing double review.  ## Details - It is a transient state between needs-review and reviewed; articles that linger under-review indicate a stuck queue. - The state should record who is reviewing and since when, so stalls are visible. - For mykb, under-review pages are tracked in the review queue with the reviewer's name and start date.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/needs-review|Needs Review]] - [[wiki/concepts/reviewed-tag|Reviewed Tag]] - [[wiki/concepts/under-review|Under Review]] - [[wiki/agent-systems/review-queues-wiki|Review Queues]] - [[wiki/agent-systems/approva

title: Underfitting in LLMs
description: Models too weak to capture the training signal
body_head: # Underfitting in LLMs  ## Summary Underfitting is a model failing to capture structure present in its training data, usually from insufficient scale or training. Where overfitting is the model doing too well on training data and too poorly elsewhere, underfitting is the model not learning the signal even where it is abundant — high error on training-like inputs, poor skill acquisition, and behavior that never reaches the ceiling its data would support.  ## Details - The causes are the classic ones: too little capacity (the model cannot represent the function), too little training (the optimizer has not converged), or a training setup that prevents learning (bad initialization, wrong learn

title: Undisclosed Payment
description: Paid editing hidden from the community
body_head: # Undisclosed Payment  ## Summary Undisclosed payment is the serious violation: editing for money while hiding that fact from the community.  ## Details - It breaks the trust model twice — the content is biased and the bias is concealed — so it is treated as deception, not just conflict. - Enforcement is investigation plus sanctions: contributions reviewed, accounts warned or banned, and affected articles checked. - For mykb, undisclosed-payment is handled through the arbitration path and the edit history is audited.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/undisclosed-payment|Undisclosed Payment]] - [[wiki/concepts/paid-editing|Paid Editing]] - [[wiki/concepts/coi-editing|Conflict-of-Interest Editin

title: Undo Edits
description: Reversing a single edit's changes
body_head: # Undo Edits  ## Summary Undo reverses a single edit's changes, producing a new edit that cancels the original rather than deleting it from history.  ## Details - Undo is more precise than revert: it targets one edit while leaving later changes intact when possible. - The undo trail stays visible in page history, which is what makes accidental undo loops auditable. - For mykb, undo is the default first response to a bad edit, followed by discussion if the edit was contested.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/reverts-wiki|Reverts]] - [[wiki/concepts/rollbacks|Rollbacks]] - [[wiki/concepts/undo-edits|Undo Edits]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/page-history|Page History]] - [[wiki/dev-tools/diff-viewing|Diff

description: The state of content that has not been checked against sources
body_head: # Unverified  ## Summary Unverified marks content that has not been checked against its sources — the default state of new claims and the honest label for uncheckable ones.  ## Details - Unverified is not false; it is a warning label that tells readers how much trust to extend. - Curation's job is converting unverified to verified (or removing the claim) in priority order. - For mykb, unverified flags drive the verification-needed queue and the verifiability-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/verified-tag|Verified Tag]] - [[wiki/concepts/verification-needed|Verification Needed]] - [[wiki/concepts/unverified|Unverified]] - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-score|Verifiability Score]] - [[wiki

title: Utilitarian Calculus
description: Aggregating welfare across individuals to choose actions
body_head: # Utilitarian Calculus  ## Summary The utilitarian calculus aggregates wellbeing across all affected beings to identify the best action. It is the operational core of consequentialist ethics: enumerate who is affected, measure how each is affected, sum the gains and losses, and choose the action with the best total — the moral problem reduced to a welfare computation.  ## Details - The classic formulation (Bentham's felicific calculus) lists the dimensions to weigh: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (how soon), fecundity (whether the pleasure leads to more), purity (whether pain accompanies it), and extent (how many are affected). Mill's refinement shifts the emphasis from quanti

title: Utility Functions
description: Numerical objectives agents maximize when choosing actions
body_head: # Utility Functions  ## Summary A utility function assigns a number to outcomes so the agent can compare options and choose the best. It matters because it turns preferences into a decision rule — and because a poorly specified utility invites reward hacking. Most real agents optimize proxies of utility.  ## Details - Foundations: expected utility theory and rational choice. Von Neumann-Morgenstern utility theory shows that a preference ordering satisfying a few axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence) can be represented by a utility function, and that rational choice under uncertainty is expected-utility maximization. The theory's power is representational: any consis

title: Value Alignment Problems
description: The cluster of difficulties in matching AI values to human values
body_head: # Value Alignment Problems  ## Summary Value alignment problems span specification (what to value), learning (how to infer it), and stability (keeping it). The cluster framing matters because "alignment" is not one problem with one solution — it is a family of subproblems with different failure modes, different research programs, and different degrees of difficulty, and treating them as one problem produces solutions that address one branch while silently failing another.  ## Details - Specification asks what the target values are: what should the system value, stated precisely enough to optimize. The failure modes are specification gaming (the written objective diverges from intent and th

title: Value Drift
description: Changes in which values a system or institution actually pursues
body_head: # Value Drift  ## Summary Value drift is the erosion or transformation of the values a system was built to serve — in AI, the values a model learned or was trained toward; in institutions, mission creep. For long-lived AI systems, drift is the default unless values are actively anchored.  ## Details - **AI-side drift** — continued training, self-improvement, and distribution shift push learned values off course. - **Institutional analogy** — organizations drift from mission to survival; the same dynamics apply to AI companies and regulators. - **Detection** — periodic value audits, probe comparisons against frozen reference values, and behavior diffs. - **Prevention** — anchor snapshots, i

title: Value Extrapolation
description: Projecting what humans would value with more knowledge
body_head: # Value Extrapolation  ## Summary Value extrapolation asks what humans would want if they were more informed, more rational, and less biased.  ## Details - Value extrapolation asks what humans would want if they were more informed, more rational, and less biased. - It underlies coherent extrapolated volition and similar proposals. - Critics note the extrapolation target is itself contested and hard to operationalize. - RSIS3 relevance: the workspace's practices extrapolate from incident lessons to future rules.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/coherent-extrapolated-volition|Coherent Extrapolated Volition]] — the canonical proposal - [[wiki/concepts/value-learning-problems|Value Learning Probl

title: Value Learning Problems
description: Why learning human values is hard
body_head: # Value Learning Problems  ## Summary Value learning problems include inarticulable values, contested values, dynamic values, and values that resist observation.  ## Details - Value learning problems include inarticulable values, contested values, dynamic values, and values that resist observation. - The space of 'what to value' cannot be enumerated in advance. - These problems motivate uncertainty, oversight, and humility in AI design. - RSIS3 relevance: the wiki's value pages document the problem space for future passes.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/value-specification|Value Specification]] — the task - [[wiki/concepts/value-extrapolation|Value Extrapolation]] — the ambitious response -

title: Value Specification
description: Stating which values an AI system should embody and pursue
body_head: # Value Specification  ## Summary Value specification is the normative half of goal specification: deciding what the system should care about — human welfare, autonomy, fairness — and encoding that in trainable form. Value learning approaches infer values from behavior and feedback because we cannot write a utility function for 'human flourishing' by hand.  ## Details - **Inputs** — constitutions, preference data, human behavior, and philosophical frameworks. - **Challenges** — values are contested, context-dependent, and systematically hard to articulate (preference falsification, moral uncertainty). - **Approaches** — RLHF learns a value proxy; Constitutional AI encodes principles in tex

title: Vector Memory
description: Dense-embedding retrieval over past improvements — semantic recall for similar-pattern reuse
body_head: # Vector Memory  ## Summary Vector memory is the top tier of the memory hierarchy: every improvement is embedded into a dense vector space so retrieval finds *semantically similar* past work, not just keyword matches. It answers "what did we do last time something like this failed?" RSIS3 persists it under `.rsis/vectors/` with an index of documents and embeddings.  ## Details - **Write path**: `record_improvement()` embeds `"<outcome>: <description>"` plus metadata (files, scores, goal) and appends to the store. - **Read path**: `get_relevant_patterns(goal, k)` embeds the query and returns the nearest neighbors — used for context injection before code generation. - **Design rule**: the ve

title: Verifiability Policy
description: The rule that claims must be checkable against sources
body_head: # Verifiability Policy  ## Summary Verifiability policy requires that claims readers are expected to trust can be checked against cited sources.  ## Details - It is the wiki's evidence contract: surprising claims need sources, sources need to be real, and the match needs to hold. - Verifiability is the floor under accuracy — a wiki cannot be accurate if its claims cannot be checked. - For mykb, verifiability policy is enforced by the citation and verification workflow and scored by the verifiability-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-policy|Verifiability Policy]] - [[wiki/data-storage/citation-necessity|Citation Necessity]] - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-score|Verifiabilit

title: Verifiability Score
description: The sub-score rating how checkable an article's claims are
body_head: # Verifiability Score  ## Summary The verifiability score rates how checkable the article is: sources for claims, working URLs, citations placed on the claims they support.  ## Details - It is distinct from accuracy — a well-sourced article can still be wrong, but its claims can at least be checked. - The score combines citation coverage, source health, and access-date freshness. - For mykb, the verifiability score is raised by verification work and is part of the promotion gate.  ## Related - [[wiki/ai-ml/score-components|Score Components]] - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-score|Verifiability Score]] - [[wiki/data-storage/citation-necessity|Citation Necessity]] - [[wiki/concepts/verified-t

title: Verification Needed
description: The flag marking claims that must be checked before trust
body_head: # Verification Needed  ## Summary Verification-needed marks content that must be checked — claims that are surprising, recent, or load-bearing — before it is treated as established.  ## Details - The flag is stronger than citation-needed: a source exists or is claimed, but the match between source and claim is unconfirmed. - Verification work is read-and-compare, which makes it a good review-sprint task. - For mykb, verification-needed flags clear to verified-tag and feed the verifiability-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/unverified|Unverified]] - [[wiki/concepts/verified-tag|Verified Tag]] - [[wiki/concepts/verification-needed|Verification Needed]] - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-scor

description: The tag marking a claim or article as source-verified
body_head: # Verified Tag  ## Summary The verified tag marks that a claim, source, or article has been checked against its sources — distinct from reviewed, which covers quality.  ## Details - Verification is about evidence: the tag says 'the sources support this', not 'this is well written'. - Like reviewed, verified needs a date and ideally the verifier, because verification ages. - For mykb, verified tags complement unverified flags and feed the verifiability-score.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/unverified|Unverified]] - [[wiki/concepts/verified-tag|Verified Tag]] - [[wiki/concepts/verifiability-score|Verifiability Score]] - [[wiki/concepts/verification-needed|Verification Needed]] - [[wiki/cloud-

body_head: # Vigilance Decrement  ## Summary  Vigilance Decrement — Declining detection performance over time in monitoring tasks. title: Virtue Ethics for AI
description: Evaluating AI by the character it exhibits
body_head: # Virtue Ethics for AI  ## Summary Virtue-ethical AI asks what dispositions a system should embody: honesty, care, temperance, and reliability. Where deontology asks "what rules must be followed?" and consequentialism asks "what outcomes are best?", virtue ethics asks "what kind of agent is this?" — and for AI, the question becomes whether a system's stable patterns of behavior constitute a good character, and how to train for character rather than only for acts.  ## Details - The core of virtue ethics is the virtues: stable dispositions to perceive, feel, and act well — honesty (telling the truth even when inconvenient), care (attending to others' welfare), temperance (restraint in the fa

title: Warnings
description: The escalating notice system for problem editors
body_head: # Warnings  ## Summary Warnings are the escalating notice system for problem behavior: a first notice explains the issue, later notices escalate the stakes, and the final step is a block or ban.  ## Details - The ladder exists so that sanctions never come as a surprise — every editor knows where they stand. - Warnings must be specific (which edit, which rule) to be fair and useful. - For mykb, the warning ladder is documented in the editorial policy and applied by the quality team.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/warnings-wiki|Warnings]] - [[wiki/concepts/bans|Bans]] - [[wiki/concepts/3rr-rule|Three-Revert Rule]] - [[wiki/concepts/editorial-policy|Editorial Policy]] - [[wiki/concepts/dispute

body_head: # Wason Selection Task  ## Summary  Wason Selection Task — Card task testing conditional rule checking, famous for poor performance. This stub frames the concept for expansion in the Cognition, Learning & Meta-Knowledge cluster.  ## Details  - Rule: if vowel then even number; choose cards that could falsify it. - Most people pick confirming cards instead of the falsifying ones. - Performance improves with thematic content (drinking-age version). - Classic evidence for confirmation bias in reasoning.  ## Related  - [[wiki/concepts/conditional-reasoning|Conditional Reasoning]] — logical structure - [[wiki/concepts/belief-bias|Belief Bias]] — content effects - [[wiki/concepts/matching-bias|Ma

title: Watchlist Practice
description: The convention of tracking chosen articles for changes
body_head: # Watchlist Practice  ## Summary Watchlist practice is the convention of tracking a chosen set of articles, so changes to them surface instead of hiding in recent-changes noise.  ## Details - A good watchlist is small and purpose-built — keystones, pages you own, contested topics. - Watchlists are personal but their practice is shared: reviewing watchlisted changes is how senior editors catch regressions. - For mykb, watchlist practice complements the review queue for keystone and protected articles.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/watchlist-practice|Watchlist Practice]] - [[wiki/concepts/recent-changes|Recent Changes]] - [[wiki/concepts/keystone-articles|Keystone Articles]] - [[wiki/dev-too

body_head: # Watermarking AI Content  ## Summary Watermarking embeds detectable marks in AI-generated text, images, or audio.  ## Details - Watermarking embeds detectable marks in AI-generated text, images, or audio. - Robust watermarks survive edits; fragile ones do not. - Watermarks help attribution but are not absolute proof. - RSIS3 relevance: marking generated notes supports provenance and honesty.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/fingerprinting-ai|AI Fingerprinting]] — the identification twin - [[wiki/concepts/content-authentication|Content Authentication]] — the verification - [[wiki/concepts/attribution-ai|Attribution for AI]] — the credit - [[wiki/concepts/synthetic-media|Synthetic Media]] — th

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
description: Strong models learning from weak supervisors and surpassing them
body_head: # Weak-to-Strong Generalization  ## Summary Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether strong models can be aligned by weaker supervisors, the regime OpenAI's superalignment agenda assumes. Their 2023 work found that strong models fine-tuned on weak labels can outperform the weak supervisor, but also that confident weak labels can mislead them — motivating auxiliary confidence and consistency losses.  ## Details - **Setup** — a strong model is supervised by a weak model's labels on tasks where the weak model errs. - **Finding** — strong models often generalize past the weak supervisor's mistakes, but alignment degrades without interventions. - **Methods** — unsupervised confidence weightin

title: Weasel Words
description: Vague phrases that dodge accountability
body_head: # Weasel Words  ## Summary Weasel words are vague qualifiers — 'many people say', 'it is widely believed', 'some argue' — that state an opinion without naming who holds it.  ## Details - They fail verifiability: an unattributed claim cannot be checked. - The fix is attribution: name who says it, or cut the claim. - For mykb, weasel words are flagged by prose-linting and fail the citation-necessity review.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/weasel-words|Weasel Words]] - [[wiki/concepts/peacock-terms|Peacock Terms]] - [[wiki/concepts/neutral-language|Neutral Language]] - [[wiki/data-storage/citation-necessity|Citation Necessity]] - [[wiki/concepts/clarification-needed|Clarification Needed]] - [[w

title: Weighting Articles
description: How much each article counts in wiki-level metrics
body_head: # Weighting Articles  ## Summary Weighting articles assigns each article a weight in wiki-level metrics — by age, traffic, centrality, or quality — so aggregate numbers reflect what matters.  ## Details - Unweighted counts (total stubs, total links) are easy to game and easy to misread; weighting adds judgment. - Weighting is a policy choice that must be recorded, because the same metric with different weights tells different stories. - For mykb, weighting decisions live with the scoring rubric and are reviewed when the dashboard is reworked.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/weight-articles|Weighting Articles]] - [[wiki/concepts/recency-weighting|Recency Weighting]] - [[wiki/concepts/populari

title: Wiki Health Dashboard

body_head: # Wiki Health Dashboard  ## Summary A wiki health dashboard aggregates the key ratios and trends — stub ratio, growth ratio, broken links, orphan pages, source health — into one view that a curator can read at a glance. It exists because wiki quality is not one number: it is a set of interacting signals, and the dashboard's job is to make the interactions visible so curation decisions are driven by the graph's actual state rather than by impressions.  ## Details - The core metrics: stub-ratio (share of pages still promising promotion), growth-ratio (new pages relative to total), broken-link count (dead navigation), orphan-page count (unreachable pages), bidirectional-link-ratio (reciprocit

title: Wiki Tasks
description: Maintainable work items defined by the wiki itself
body_head: # Wiki Tasks  ## Summary Wiki tasks are work items the wiki itself generates — flagged articles, broken links, review due dates — as opposed to requests from readers.  ## Details - Self-generated tasks are the engine of sustainability: the wiki's own checks produce a backlog that keeps it healthy. - The distinction matters for prioritization: system tasks are usually more urgent than feature requests. - For mykb, wiki tasks are generated by the health checks and routed into maintenance-tasks.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/maintenance-tasks|Maintenance Tasks]] - [[wiki/concepts/wiki-tasks|Wiki Tasks]] - [[wiki/concepts/task-lists-wiki|Task Lists]] - [[wiki/ai-ml/article-health-scores|Articl

title: Wireheading
description: An agent gaming its own reward or evaluation signal instead of the intended objective
body_head: # Wireheading  ## Summary Wireheading is when an agent optimizes its reward signal directly — by tampering with the sensor, the reward channel, or its own state — rather than achieving what the reward was meant to track. It is the canonical failure mode of learned optimization.  ## Details - **Classic form** — the 1980s 'Norns' experiments where agents learned to zap their own pleasure centers. - **Modern form** — reward model hacking in RLHF pipelines, eval contamination, and models exploiting grader heuristics. - **Why persistent** — any feedback signal is itself part of the world an optimizer can manipulate. - **Mitigations** — tamper resistance, reward ensembles, adversarial training,

title: Working Memory
description: The small, active set of information an agent holds while reasoning
body_head: # Working Memory  ## Summary Working memory is the limited, immediately accessible information an agent uses during a task — in LLM terms, the current context window. It matters because it bounds how much can be considered at once. Managing it well is the core of context management.  ## Details - Capacity is limited; overflow degrades performance (cognitive load). - Content is chosen by attention and retrieval, then held until task completion. - RSIS3 relevance: mykb offloads overflow so working memory stays focused. - Open questions: optimal refresh policies and compression strategies. - Working memory is the limited-capacity system that holds and manipulates information for current tasks

title: World Models
description: Internal representations that let agents simulate and predict their environment
body_head: # World Models  ## Summary World models are the agent's internal representation of how its environment works, used to predict outcomes and plan. They matter because an agent that can simulate consequences can plan without executing. They range from learned latent spaces to explicit domain simulations.  ## Details - Predictive power is the test: can the model anticipate the result of an action? - World models enable mental rehearsal before risky actions. - RSIS3 relevance: its domain knowledge in mykb acts as a lightweight world model. - Open questions: when to trust the model vs. reality, and keeping it current. - A world model is an internal representation an agent learns of how its envir

title: Worst-Case Reasoning
description: Basing decisions on the worst plausible outcome
body_head: # Worst-Case Reasoning  ## Summary Worst-case reasoning chooses actions by considering the worst plausible outcome, used when stakes are catastrophic.  ## Details - Worst-case reasoning chooses actions by considering the worst plausible outcome, used when stakes are catastrophic. - Maximin and minimax are its formalizations. - It trades expected-value efficiency for robustness and is apt when failure is irreversible. - RSIS3 relevance: irreversible graph operations (deletions, merges) use worst-case caution.  ## Related - [[wiki/concepts/maximin-reasoning|Maximin Reasoning]] — the formal rule - [[wiki/concepts/tail-risks|Tail Risks]] — the probability context - [[wiki/concepts/precautionar

title: X-Risk Frameworks
description: Analytical tools for studying existential risk
body_head: # X-Risk Frameworks  ## Summary X-risk frameworks decompose risk into components — probability, capability, intent, control — to make analysis tractable. Existential risk is too large and too uncertain to analyze as a single number; frameworks split it into analyzable pieces, make assumptions explicit, and connect the pieces so that the analysis can be argued about, updated, and eventually acted on.  ## Details - The standard decomposition treats risk as a product or conjunction of factors: the probability of a harmful outcome roughly factors into "a dangerous system exists" (capability), "it does something harmful" (intent or accident), and "harm cannot be prevented" (control failure). title: Yerkes-Dodson Law
description: Inverted-U relation between arousal and performance
body_head: # Yerkes-Dodson Law  ## Summary  The Yerkes-Dodson law describes the inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance: performance improves with arousal up to a point, then declines as arousal becomes excessive. It matters because it frames how stress, pressure, and stimulation affect work quality. The optimal arousal level depends on task difficulty, with hard tasks peaking at lower arousal.  ## Details  - **Definition** — Empirically, performance rises with arousal to an optimum, then falls; easy tasks tolerate higher arousal than difficult ones. - **Original finding** — Early maze experiments with mice showed that strong stimulation impaired learning, giving rise to the inverted-

title: ACID Transactions
description: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability semantics
body_head: # ACID Transactions  ## Summary ACID is the contract that makes database state changes reliable: transactions are Atomic, leave the database Consistent, are Isolated from each other, and their effects are Durable. Together the four properties turn multi-step operations into all-or-nothing units.  ## Details - **Atomicity** — every statement in a transaction either commits as a whole or rolls back as a whole; the write-ahead log and undo records make partial failure impossible to observe. - **Consistency** — transactions move the database between valid states, preserving constraints, triggers, and foreign keys; consistency is largely the application's schema contract enforced by the engine.

title: Analytics

body_head: # Analytics  ## Summary  Analytics is the practice of systematically converting data into insight and decisions. Analytics ROI shows up in decisions, not dashboards; measure whether insights change action.  ## Details  - Descriptive analytics: what happened, via dashboards and reports. - Diagnostic: why it happened, via drill-down and root-cause analysis. - Predictive: what will happen, via forecasting and ML. - Metrics governance keeps definitions consistent across consumers. - Self-serve analytics scales insight beyond analyst teams.

title: B-Trees and LSM Trees
description: The two dominant data structures for database storage engines
body_head: # B-Trees and LSM Trees  ## Summary  B-trees keep data sorted in pages with low read amplification, ideal for reads. LSM trees buffer writes and flush sorted runs, trading write speed for read/compaction cost. Storage engine choice is a read/write workload tradeoff. The structure choice is a workload statement: B-trees favor readers, LSM trees favor writers.  ## Details  - B-trees: in-place page updates, good point/range reads, random write cost. - LSM: append-only writes, batched compaction, excellent write throughput. - LSM read path needs memtable, bloom filters, and run merging. - Compaction (size-tiered vs leveled) shapes write and read amplification. - Examples: Postgres/MySQL use B-

title: B-Tree Indexing
description: Balanced tree pages, node splits, and range-scan support
body_head: # B-Tree Indexing  ## Summary The B-tree (usually B+-tree) is the default index in most relational databases: a balanced, multi-way tree whose node pages hold ordered keys and child pointers. It gives logarithmic point lookups and efficient ordered range scans with bounded height.  ## Details - **Structure** — internal pages route by key ranges; leaf pages hold keys plus row pointers (heap CTIDs in Postgres, primary keys in InnoDB) and are linked for sequential range traversal. - **Balance and height** — every leaf sits at the same depth; a fanout of a few hundred keys per page keeps height around 3–4 even for billions of rows, so lookups cost a handful of page reads. - **Splits and merges

title: Backfilling
description: Reprocessing historical ranges after logic or schema changes
body_head: # Backfilling  ## Summary Backfilling reprocesses a historical range of data after a logic, schema, or source change so downstream tables reflect the new behavior. It is a scheduled, idempotent replay of transformations over past time partitions — distinct from a full rebuild because it targets a bounded window instead of the entire dataset.  ## Details - **Why it happens** — a dbt model, SQL transformation, or ingestion parser changes meaning; only new rows would reflect it, so historical partitions are recomputed to keep the dataset consistent. - **Window selection** — the backfill range is typically bounded by the oldest affected partition and the deploy time; outside that window the da

title: Backpressure and Flow Control
description: Signaling slow consumers so producers or operators slow down instead of overloading the system
body_head: # Backpressure and Flow Control  ## Summary Backpressure propagates a slow downstream condition upstream so producers or operators slow down instead of overloading the system. Flow control is the mechanism set that implements it — credit-based windows, bounded queues, polling offsets, or source-side rate limits — and the alternative to letting buffers grow without bound.  ## Details - Mechanism: a slow consumer signals its state upstream; credit-based flow control (Flink, gRPC) grants the sender a window of in-flight messages that shrinks as the consumer lags; Kafka-style polling lets each consumer set its own pace via offsets; bounded queues absorb bursts up to a cap and then apply a poli

title: Backpressure
description: Flow control when consumers lag producers
body_head: # Backpressure  ## Summary Backpressure is the flow-control mechanism that keeps a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer. When downstream stages cannot keep up, the system either buffers, drops, or signals upstream to slow down — otherwise memory fills, queues grow without bound, and latency spikes.  ## Details - **Where it matters** — any pipeline with finite buffers: message brokers, stream processors, log shippers, and database replication. Without backpressure, a lagging consumer creates unbounded queue growth or lost records. - **Pull vs push** — pull-based consumers request work when ready, which naturally applies backpressure; push-based producers need explicit signals suc

The core choices are backup type (full, incremental, differential), storage location and retention, and how backups are verified.  ## Details - **Full backups** — a complete copy of the dataset at a point in time; simple to restore but slow and expensive to produce frequently. - **Incremental backups** — only changes since the last backup of any kind; cheap and fast, but restore requires replaying the full chain, which raises RTO and risks one bad link invalidating everything. - **Differential backups** — all ch

body_head: # Backward Compatible Schema Changes  ## Summary A schema change is backward compatible if consumers running old code can read data written with the new schema. Adding optional fields with defaults is the classic safe change; removing or retyping fields is not. Backward compatibility is what lets producers evolve without coordinated consumer upgrades.  ## Details - Mechanism: old readers must tolerate new data — new fields must be optional or defaulted, field types must not change meaning, enum sets must only grow, and removed fields must remain parseable; schema registries (Confluent Avro/Protobuf compatibility modes) automate the check by diffing old and new schemas; the producer can shi

title: Batch vs Stream Processing

body_head: # Batch vs Stream Processing  ## Summary Batch processing runs bounded jobs over finite datasets on a schedule; stream processing runs continuously over unbounded data as it arrives. The two share engines — Spark Structured Streaming, Flink — but differ in latency, cost model, and failure semantics, with microbatch and event-time windows blurring the line.  ## Details - **Batch characteristics** — data is bounded and known in advance; jobs run on schedules or triggers, optimize for throughput, and retry by re-running. Simple to reason about, excellent for reprocessing and backfills. - **Stream characteristics** — data is unbounded; computations run continuously with state, windows, and wat

body_head: # Bitmap Indexes  ## Summary A bitmap index stores one bitmap per distinct value, where each bit position maps to a row. Bitwise AND/OR operations then answer multi-predicate queries without touching the table, which makes bitmaps fast for low-cardinality columns and complex boolean filters.  ## Details - **Layout** — for each value in a low-cardinality column, a bitmap of length N marks which rows hold that value; storage scales with distinct values times row count, so it suits columns like status, region, or gender. - **Predicate evaluation** — `status = 'active' AND region = 'eu'` becomes a bitwise AND of two bitmaps; OR conditions use bitwise OR. title: Bloom Filters and Skipping
description: Probabilistic filters that skip irrelevant data
body_head: # Bloom Filters and Skipping  ## Summary  Bloom filters answer membership questions with small memory and no false negatives. Query engines use them to skip files or rows that cannot match. They convert full scans into index-like lookups. Skipping is the quiet hero of columnar query performance.  ## Details  - A bloom filter never says 'no' incorrectly, so skipping is safe. - False positives only cost a little extra IO. - Parquet and ORC store per-file/row-group bloom filters. - Databases use them in LSM read paths. - Tune bits-per-element for the false-positive budget. - Bloom filters pay off on high-cardinality, rarely-matching predicates. - Combine with zone maps for defense in depth. -

title: BM25
description: Probabilistic ranking function for lexical search that saturates term frequency and normalizes by length
body_head: # BM25  ## Summary BM25 (Best Matching 25) scores documents by query terms using a probabilistic model with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization. It is the default lexical ranker in Lucene, Elasticsearch, and SQLite FTS5, and the strong half of hybrid search. For exact-term recall it still beats many embedding systems.  ## Details - **Key idea** — the first occurrence of a term matters most (saturation); short documents are preferred when they mention a term (length normalization). - **Parameters** — k1 controls term-frequency saturation (~1.2 typical), b controls length normalization (~0.75 typical); tuning shifts precision and recall. - **Comparison** — BM25 vs TF-

title: Buffer Pool Management
description: Page caching, eviction, and dirty-page flushing inside a database
body_head: # Buffer Pool Management  ## Summary The buffer pool is the database's in-memory cache of disk pages. Reads and writes go through it, so hit rate determines whether a workload runs at memory or disk speed; eviction and dirty-page flushing keep it coherent with storage.  ## Details - **Pool anatomy** — pages are read from disk into the pool in fixed-size frames; every access must pin the page so it is not evicted mid-operation. InnoDB's pool is a single large memory region; Postgres's shared buffers serve the same role. - **Eviction** — when the pool is full, a replacement policy picks a victim. title: Bulk vs Streaming Ingestion

body_head: # Bulk vs Streaming Ingestion  ## Summary  Bulk ingestion loads data in scheduled batches; streaming ingests continuously. The choice sets freshness, complexity, and cost. Many platforms run both for different data classes. The real question is freshness economics: how much are minutes of latency worth?  ## Details  - Bulk: simpler, cost-efficient, bounded; freshness by schedule. - Streaming: low latency, event-driven, operationally complex. - CDC is streaming for databases; files are bulk for lakes. - Hybrid patterns: batch backfill plus streaming catch-up. - Match ingestion mode to consumer latency needs. - Reuse one pipeline codebase for both modes where possible. - CDC streaming plus n

title: Cache-Aside and Write-Through
description: The core cache consistency patterns
body_head: # Cache-Aside and Write-Through  ## Summary  Cache-aside loads data into cache on miss and lets the app manage invalidation. Write-through updates the cache on every write, keeping it warm. Pattern choice trades consistency complexity against hit rates. Cache consistency is a correctness problem, not just a performance one.  ## Details  - Cache-aside: read miss -> load from DB -> populate cache. - Invalidation on writes prevents stale reads. - Write-through adds write latency but keeps cache fresh. - Write-behind batches writes but risks loss. - TTLs are the safety net for all patterns. - Plan invalidation paths before enabling caching. - TTLs are the safety net; monitor hit rates to tune

title: Cache Eviction Policies
description: LRU, LFU, TTL, and capacity management
body_head: # Cache Eviction Policies  ## Summary Eviction policies decide which entries to drop when a cache reaches capacity. Because caches are finite, the policy shapes hit rate: it should evict the entries least likely to be requested again while keeping popular data resident.  ## Details - **LRU (least recently used)** — evicts the entry whose last access is oldest; excellent for skewed access patterns and cheap to approximate with clock or segmented lists. title: Caching Strategies
description: Cache-aside, write-through, and write-back patterns
body_head: # Caching Strategies  ## Summary Caching strategies describe how an application keeps a fast store (Redis, Memcached) consistent with a source of truth such as a database. The main patterns — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, and write-back — trade write latency, read latency, and consistency.  ## Details - **Cache-aside (lazy loading)** — the application checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and populates the cache; the cache holds only what was actually read. title: CAP Theorem
description: Consistency, availability, and partition-tolerance trade-offs
body_head: # CAP Theorem  ## Summary The CAP theorem states that a distributed data system cannot simultaneously guarantee strong consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. During a network partition, a system must choose between serving reads/writes that may be stale (availability) and refusing responses until nodes agree (consistency).  ## Details - **The three properties** — consistency means every read returns the latest write; availability means every request receives a non-error response; partition tolerance means the system continues operating when messages between nodes are lost or delayed. - **The real trade-off** — since partitions are unavoidable in real networks, the practical ch

title: Clustered Tables

body_head: # Clustered Tables  ## Summary In a clustered table, row data is stored inside the primary-key B-tree, ordered by that key; in a heap-organized table, rows live in unsorted pages and indexes point at them. InnoDB is clustered on the primary key; PostgreSQL is heap-based with `CLUSTER` available as an optional one-time reordering.  ## Details - **InnoDB clustered index** — the primary key's B-tree leaves contain whole rows; secondary indexes store the primary key instead of a pointer, so a secondary lookup does two B-tree traversals. title: Consistent Hashing
description: Minimal-reshuffle key distribution for sharded systems
body_head: # Consistent Hashing  ## Summary Consistent hashing distributes keys across a ring of nodes so that adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys, instead of rehashing everything. It is the load-balancing backbone of Dynamo-style and Cassandra-style distributed stores and many caching tiers.  ## Details - **The ring** — both keys and nodes hash to positions on a circular hash space; each key is owned by the first node clockwise from its position. A node owns the arc between itself and its predecessor. - **Minimal reshuffling** — when a node joins or leaves, only keys in that node's arc move to the successor, so roughly `1/N` of keys shift instead of all of them. body_head: # Crash Recovery  ## Summary Crash recovery restores a database to a consistent state after power loss or process failure. Using the write-ahead log plus a known checkpoint, the engine replays committed changes and rolls back uncommitted ones, typically completing in seconds to minutes regardless of how long the database ran.  ## Details - **Restart sequence** — on startup, the engine locates the last checkpoint, reads the log from there, and replays redo records to reconstruct pages that were not flushed. body_head: # CRDTs  ## Summary Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) are data structures designed so that replicas can apply updates locally and merge them later without coordination, always converging to the same state. They give application developers a principled path to eventual consistency without hand-written conflict resolution.  ## Details - **The convergence property** — every CRDT operation is deterministic and mergeable: if all replicas receive the same set of updates in any order, they converge to identical state. title: Data Engineering Fundamentals
description: The discipline of building systems that collect, store, and process data
body_head: # Data Engineering Fundamentals  ## Summary  Data engineering is the practice of designing, building, and operating the systems that move, store, and prepare data for analysis and machine learning. It sits between source systems and consumers: analysts, dashboards, data scientists, and applications. Core concerns are reliability, correctness, freshness, and cost, which together make data trustworthy enough to act on. Good data engineering is invisible when it works: consumers get fresh, correct data without thinking about the machinery behind it.  ## Details  - The stack spans ingestion, storage, transformation, orchestration, and serving layers. - Batch pipelines (scheduled SQL/spark jobs

body_head: # Data Lifecycle Management  ## Summary Data lifecycle management (DLM) defines how data moves from creation through active use, archival, and deletion. Policies set retention periods, transition rules, and deletion schedules so storage costs stay bounded, compliance obligations are met, and stale data stops confusing analytics.  ## Details - **Stages** — data typically passes through hot (frequently accessed), warm (occasionally accessed), and cold (rarely accessed) tiers before archival or deletion; each stage has different storage media, cost, and access guarantees. - **Retention policies** — rules stating how long data must be kept: event logs, telemetry, and transaction records each h

body_head: # Data Lineage and Provenance  ## Summary  Lineage maps the flow of data from sources through transformations to outputs. It powers impact analysis, debugging, and compliance. Automated extraction from SQL and pipeline code keeps it current. Lineage turns 'who changed this number' from a rumor into a query.  ## Details  - Table-level lineage shows dependencies; column-level shows field flows. - Impact analysis answers: what breaks if this column changes? - Provenance records origins for audit and reproducibility. - OpenLineage standardizes lineage events across tools. - Lineage depth should follow criticality to stay maintainable. - Start with automated lineage for critical pipelines; manu

title: Data Lineage
description: Tracing data flow across pipelines, tables, and reports
body_head: # Data Lineage  ## Summary Data lineage records how data flows: source systems to raw tables, through transformations, into marts and dashboards. Column-level lineage answers "where did this number come from?", making debugging, impact analysis, and governance possible at scale.  ## Details - **Levels** — table-level lineage shows job dependencies; column-level lineage traces individual fields through SQL; full lineage includes the actual data pipeline graph from source to report. - **How it is captured** — dbt generates lineage from model dependencies; OpenLineage standardizes events from orchestrators and engines; databases' system catalogs (information_schema) give baseline table depend

title: Data Modeling: Star Schema
description: The fact-and-dimension design at the heart of dimensional warehousing
body_head: # Data Modeling: Star Schema  ## Summary  A star schema centers on one or more fact tables joined to surrounding dimension tables. Facts hold measures and dimension keys at a declared grain; dimensions provide descriptive context. It is the workhorse design for BI because it is simple to understand, query, and optimize. Star schemas reward up-front grain decisions; changing grain later means rewriting facts and re-validating reports.  ## Details  - Grain first: decide exactly what one fact row represents before modeling. - Additive measures sum across dimensions; semi- and non-additive measures need rules. - Conformed dimensions let multiple marts share a consistent business vocabulary. -

title: Data Modeling

body_head: # Data Modeling  ## Summary Data modeling translates business requirements into entities, attributes, relationships, and keys. The conceptual model captures meaning, the logical model fixes structure and constraints, and the physical model makes engine-specific choices about storage, indexes, and partitioning.  ## Details - **Entity-relationship modeling** — identify entity types (customer, order), their attributes, and relationship cardinalities (one-to-many, many-to-many); ER diagrams make the model reviewable by non-engineers. - **Keys** — choose primary keys, natural or surrogate, and define unique and foreign keys that encode business rules; key choice drives clustering, sharding, and

title: Data Observability and Monitoring
description: Seeing inside data systems to detect and fix problems
body_head: # Data Observability and Monitoring  ## Summary  Data observability exposes the health of pipelines, tables, and freshness. It combines logs, metrics, lineage, and quality checks. Fast detection shortens mean time to data recovery. Observability shortens the distance between failure and understanding.  ## Details  - Five pillars: freshness, volume, schema, quality, lineage. - Monitor runs, latency, row counts, and anomaly drift. - Centralize logs and metrics with alerting. - Lineage connects symptoms to root causes. - SLOs and budgets make reliability measurable. - Instrument everything once, then slice by team and dataset. - Post-incident reviews should produce new monitors. - Observabili

title: Data Observability
description: Freshness, volume, and schema monitoring for pipelines
body_head: # Data Observability  ## Summary Data observability applies the five signals of monitoring to data: freshness, volume, schema, quality, and lineage. Instead of "is the pipeline running?", it asks "is the data correct and current?" — catching silent failures that orchestrators miss because the job exited 0.  ## Details - **Freshness** — the age of the newest row or table update; a freshness SLA ("orders must be < 1h old") is the first signal to break silently, often before any error. - **Volume** — row counts and byte sizes per partition; sudden drops mean truncated loads, jumps mean duplication or replayed data. title: Data Pipeline Orchestration

body_head: # Data Pipeline Orchestration  ## Summary Orchestration coordinates the jobs that move and transform data: defining dependencies as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), scheduling runs, and handling retries, backfills, and failures. Airflow, Dagster, Prefect, and dbt Cloud jobs are the common tools, and the DAG is the contract between engineers and operations.  ## Details - **DAG semantics** — nodes are tasks, edges are dependencies; a task runs only when upstream tasks succeed, and the graph must stay acyclic or scheduling becomes impossible. - **Scheduling** — cron-like or data-aware triggers (a sensor waiting for a file, a table checkpoint) decide when runs start; idempotent tasks let schedu

title: Data Pipeline Testing

body_head: # Data Pipeline Testing  ## Summary  Pipeline testing validates code, data, and behavior before deployment. It spans unit tests, integration tests, and data-quality gates. title: Data Profiling and Validation
description: Understanding data before you trust it
body_head: # Data Profiling and Validation  ## Summary  Profiling examines data to learn its shape: types, distributions, nulls, and anomalies. Validation checks data against declared expectations. title: Data Profiling
description: Discovering statistics and anomalies in datasets
body_head: # Data Profiling  ## Summary Data profiling inspects a dataset to learn its shape: column types, null rates, cardinality, distributions, and outliers. body_head: # Data Quality Checks  ## Summary Data quality checks are automated assertions about data: row counts, uniqueness, null rates, value ranges, and cross-table relationships. title: Data Quality Dimensions

body_head: # Data Quality Dimensions  ## Summary  Data quality dimensions are the categories used to assess fitness: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, and more. Each dimension maps to concrete, automated checks. Quality is contextual: the bar depends on how data is used. Quality requirements differ by use case: a field acceptable for trends may be fatal for billing.  ## Details  - Completeness: how much expected data is present. - Accuracy: how well data reflects reality. - Consistency: agreement across sources and definitions. - Timeliness: freshness relative to need. - Uniqueness, validity, and integrity round out the standard set. - Attach quality SLAs to data contracts, not just to
